INVITATIONS TO UNVEILING OF PLAQUE COMMEMORATING CANADA GAMES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering statements made recently at the Can-Am Bowl in Florida by the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) to the effect that the Liberal government had announced its own form of California's Proposition 13 with its recent cutbacks in fiscal spending, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle):
That the minister be compelled to explain to this House and the people of Canada why her department issued an extravagant 10 x 14 inch glossy invitation requiring a 50-cent stamp to the unveiling of a commemorative plaque in Winnipeg on February 2 in connection with the Canada Games, when a standard size invitation requiring only 14 cents postage would have been equally appropriate and considerably less expensive.

subsubtopic: HEALTH SERVICES FOR CANADIAN INDIANS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the Department of National Health and Welfare has entered into agreements with numerous band councils for the delivery of health services-for example, the Mohawks at the Bay of Quinte and the Kettle Point Reserves-and in view of the fact that the minister's recent health guidelines are in violation of the agreements and will
adversely affect the delivery of health care, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That the minister immediately place a moratorium on the guidelines to permit adequate consultation as defined in the agreements.

AVAILABILITY OF HEALTH SERVICES FOR CANADIAN INDIANS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the preceding motion was on a similar subject, its rejection does not preclude the motion I am about to move.
Considering that Canada's Indian population has the highest infant mortality rate, the highest rate of infectious diseases, the highest respiratory disease rate and the lowest level of income in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House instructs the Minister of National Health and Welfare to restore immediately health services to Canadian Indians to the level they enjoyed prior to the cutbacks recently announced so that health care is available without qualification.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Since certain publicity-seeking societies in the United States have commenced a campaign to persuade Americans not to travel to Canada until such time as Canada outlaws the seal hunt carried on off Newfoundland and in the Gulf since time immemorial, and in view of the fact that this campaign can have no worse effects on the tourism industry in Canada than the general incompetence of the government with respect to tourism, as exemplified by the increase in the air transportation tax recently announced, and in view of the fact that while the American animal protection groups campaign against the Newfoundland seal hunt, the seal hunt for adult seals killed by gunfire continues in the Alaskan islands so that furriers can be supplied with Alaskan seal furs to make into fashionable coats exported to Canada, among other countries, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies):
That the government forbid the importation of Alaskan seal furs or any article of clothing made from Alaskan seal furs until such time as the Americans cease their hypocrisy and cease their attempts to harm the livelihood of hundreds of Canadian fishermen.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT STRATEGY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Prime Minister. In view of the Prime Minister's replies yesterday that the president of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women was either unequivocally not addressing her remarks to the government in her speech of January 10, or that she was unequivocally wrong, and since an examination of her speech makes it obvious that her remarks were directed to the government and its policies regarding the employment of women in the labour force, can the Prime Minister tell the House just what state-
January 24, 1979

ments of Madame Rousseau were, indeed, unequivocally wrong?
Was she wrong when she said that the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, the government's own body to advise it on women's issues, had not been consulted before women were excluded from its employment strategy, or was she wrong in her presentation of the figures?

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT STRATEGY OF GOVERNMENT

Mr. Speaker, the hon. lady would have the answer to her question if she read the question asked by her seatmate, the hon. member for Egmont, yesterday. He made some allegations purportedly based on the statement of the hon. lady, the president of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, which I inadvertently called the Voice of Women yesterday. He made these quotes and 1 said that they were quite wrong. I still maintain that they are wrong, and I challenged Madame Rousseau or the hon. lady from Kingston to quote any evidence to the contrary.
The allegation refers to "official statements"-presumably government statements, if that is the context-and reads as follows:
-in "official statements" women are considered either "responsible for the high rate of unemployment" or are being "used as scapegoats and as a screen for a chronic inability to redress the economy"-
This is not true. No one on that side or on Mrs. Rousseau's side can quote any evidence indicating that the ministers have said that. I know the opposition has attempted to deform the truth by alleging that, but they have never brought forward any evidence of that.

speechtext: Shame.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. I want to assure him in advance that it is direct and to the point, and I just hope that his answer will be the same.
The Toronto-Dominion Bank has announced an increase in its Chargex lending rate to a scandalously high level of 21 per cent. The other chartered banks have already indicated that they will follow suit. In light of this situation, and in terms of the Prime Minister's responsibility for over-all government policy, I would like to ask him if he will call in the heads of the banks and obtain a commitment from them immediately that they will take steps to roll back these totally unwarranted increases which will force up the already high cost of living for Canadians.

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, January 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen (for Mr. Trudeau) that Bill C-35, respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather regrettable that this bill has taken the form in which it has been presented to the House. I think it would have been quite easy for the opposition to have assured the government that had this been presented as a simple bill to establish a minister of fisheries, such a bill could have received speedy consideration in the House and would have been subject to very little debate.
This House has been waiting some time for the opportunity to give serious consideration to some of the problems pertaining to the fishing industry, and while the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry has met on occasions when it had to, it has also had to deal with other business pertaining to the multitude of facets of this government which the committee considered. It has therefore been virtually impossible to get an extended opportunity to question the minister in respect of the fishing industry per se. Therefore, it could have been a very welcome opportunity, had a bill establishing a minister of fisheries been presented to the committee, to have considered such a bill.
In view of the fact that we have a pot-pourri of legislation tucked into one cover which covers many facets of government reorganization and does not relate solely to fisheries, it has become, so far as I am concerned, a subject of debate both as it relates to fisheries and to forestry. It could have been much more conveniently and expeditiously handled had this bill not been a handful of bills under one cover. But this seems to be the path which the government has chosen to follow during the past ten years. It has defied the House of Commons and defied us in this bill, in the banking legislation and in a number of other instances, with the enumeration of which I will not bore this House.
In view of the fact that this bill is a whole package wrapped up in one cover, it makes it necessary that certain facets of the government and its policies related to both fisheries and forestry become a matter of debate in the House when they
Government Organization
might very well have been debated in the committee very quickly without detriment to normal procedure in the House.
The government has been told repeatedly that this is the wrong method to obtain quick passage of both what they and we consider to be important and pertinent legislation, but it is indicative of the government's tendency and that of the Liberal party as a whole to be so sure of itself in power that it shall dictate to all those who participate in the House just how they want things to be done, without any consideration for other interested parties.
For that reason the bill has become an issue which will be debated to some extent. I should like to say to the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Faour), who has not been in the House very long, that when he referred to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) in his introductory speech on this bill as having nothing constructive to offer, he should have been aware of the fact that this party has shown historically that it has been constructive, that it has provided leadership, initiative and suggestions for improvement in policies both in the field of fisheries and forestry year after year. In fact, it was a Conservative government which established a department of forestry and a Liberal government which removed that department by amalgamating it with two others.

I do not really object to interjections; I enjoy debate and argument. Perhaps Mr. Speaker can extend my time to compensate for the interjections of the hon. member, and then the hon. member can have all the time he requires. I enjoy debating with the hon. member.
To come back to the comments of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's -St. Barbe, it was a Conservative government which established the department of forestry. It was a Liberal government which made a conglomeration of environment, forestry and fisheries which did not work. It was a Conservative opposition which pleaded with the government to re-establish the department of forestry ever since it was abandoned, and to re-establish ever since it was abandoned the department of fisheries as a separate department. That is the prestige which the industry and management needs, and that is a constructive suggestion. It has been primarily through the committee work of the opposition that the Minister of Fisher-

ies and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) was led to establish the various programs presently in place. We are still out in front.
As was mentioned by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), by fisheries ministers in the Atlantic provinces and by fishermen in their presentations to government, we need a fleet renewal program and do not have one. There is no means by which we can find the money to expand that fleet, even on a loan basis. We are out in front of the Grits and the Socialists in this regard; we have led them all the way.
The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment proposed to establish something similar to the Central Mortgage and Housing proposition. This was recommended by the hon. member for South Shore. So far it has not been established. The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment assured us that there would be plenty of money for subsidies, boat replacements and renewals. So far fishermen are not permitted to buy certain boats and the Central Mortgage and Housing type structure has not been established. Fishermen are sailing dangerous boats. They cannot afford to replace their boats under the present structure, particularly with 14 per cent, 15 per cent, 16 per cent and 17 per cent rates of interest they would be required to pay if they borrowed money through normal channels.
I suggest the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe should take a careful look at the record to see what his predecessor did and said on behalf of the fishing industry and the seal hunt. He should take a look at what the present minister of fisheries of Newfoundland said on behalf of the fishermen and what he proposed when he was a member of the House. Instead of criticizing what has not been put forward, perhaps the hon. member should criticize the government for what has not been adopted. That would be much more in line.
Because a former member of this House, the present minister of fisheries in Newfoundland, proposed a developmental program for Newfoundland, Atlantic Canada and fisheries, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have scoffed and scorned at those suggestions. They even suggested that they knew nothing about the suggestions long after they had hit the press. Perhaps the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe would do a little reading of history and get his facts straight.
Another matter which continues to concern me is the fact that young people in Atlantic Canada cannot obtain fishing licences. There is no flexibility in the quotas allowed by the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment, and there is no opportunity for young people to become involved other than the hard way-by buying out someone else. The industry has survived ever since the earliest explorers arrived on the shores of this continent. It was based upon the belief that today a man could fish and retire so that tomorrow or the next day his son may take over; or that if a man worked in a crew on a fishing vessel and decided to purchase his own boat and become his own boss, a licence would be available.
I am aware that things have not always been as they are today. We were not always as conscious as we are today about
January 24, 1979

fish supply. Also I am aware that some of the requests for licences being made by inshore fishermen would be an inconsequential addition to the present catch. For the sake of providing young and interested people with opportunities to participate in the fishing industry, we require more leniency, flexibility and adjustability in the issuance of licences for fishing on the Atlantic coast. That is a must.
I have cited an example of a man who could become involved in the fishing industry only by purchasing a very old boat which perhaps was not quite safe to sail, yet certainly very expensive to maintain. Because of a regulatory stricture that a man must own a boat for five or six years before he can replace it, with or without assistance, subsidy or loan from the Government of Canada, that man cannot replace his boat even though he owns both the boat and has a licence. This is where we get into the problem of regulations and why we should not be governed by regulations in fisheries or in any other aspect of our society.
I am very much in sympathy with families who have historically fished and who, by virtue of circumstances beyond their control, have been compelled to leave the fishing industry for one, two, three, four, five or six years on some occasions. This may have been for reasons of health, for financial reasons or for family reasons. But whatever those reasons may have been, having left that industry that family can no longer make a re-entry even though the personal circumstances may have changed. Further consideration should be given to these things and I trust that the minister will soften his program.
Once again I make a public appeal to the minister to undertake a surveillance program in the lobster and salmon fisheries that will be effective, particularly in the Atlantic area. We cannot and never will have a commercial fishing industry in Atlantic Canada with the importance it once had as long as poaching goes on at the rate reported today. This is something upon which Statistics Canada does not give us figures. It is rather unfortunate that it does not, but this is something that goes under the table rather than above the table. This does not come under regulation and cannot seem to be regulated or controlled by the government in any way.
The consequences of our lack of surveillance was made perfectly clear to an interparliamentary committee which went to Europe. While we have complained in Canada about the overfishing of salmon on the high seas, the members of that interparliamentary committee which went from this place to visit with members of parliament in Europe were assured by those members of parliament that in no way were they even going to consider negotiation on the fishing of salmon on the high seas until Canada introduced an effective surveillance program of its immediate offshore and freshwater streams.
These are items which I think are of major importance and which the committee should have had an opportunity to discuss. Instead of this bill going to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, the original suggestion was that it should go to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Esti-
Governmertt Organization
mates. That would not give a fisherman much chance to present his point of view or to promote the best interests of the fishing industry. Where it may end up now I am not sure.
The hon. member for South Shore has handled matters pertaining to the fishing industry much better than I am capable of doing because he has fished, and that gives him an expertise which none of the rest of us could possibly posses. However, there are a few things about the bill I wish to mention. The first I should like to refer to is this wrap-up clause 33 which provides for certain possibilities in respect of the transition of duties, responsibilities and functions.
What disturbs me is that this bill has not properly defined all of the fields in which the minister may function. By virtue of the fact that this has not been done, there appears a phrase at the end of the bill in clause 33 which states what shall be done by the deputy minister of fisheries and oceans. Let me quote from line 19 as follows:
-or the appropriate officer of the department of fisheries and oceans, as the case may be, unless the governor in council by order designates another minister, deputy minister or officer of a department or a portion of the Public Service of Canada to exercise such power, duty or function.
I deplore that clause in this bill as it introduces the usual uncertainty which applies to any piece of legislation this government introduces. While it is not the regulatory basket clause that is usually there, it does leave a degree of flexibility for government movement after the establishment of a ministry of fisheries, a degree of flexibility which I fear. I do not know what authority they may give or take from him because of the flexibility there.
One of the great weaknesses of the Department of Fisheries being with the Department of the Environment was that there was no such thing as a deputy minister of fisheries per se throughout most of the period of this combination of responsibilities. Too often the result was that, since there was a deputy minister of the Department of the Environment, that deputy minister was environmentally oriented. I have no quarrel with any man choosing his profession or choosing his items and the order of priorities which those items are given in his own mind. What I do quarrel with, and what I did quarrel with under the old structure, is that there being no equal of a deputy minister on behalf of fisheries the Department of the Environment imposed regulations upon fisheries which were unnecessary and burdensome to that industry.
We now find that the department of forestry is to be put in exactly the same position. That department will find itself combined with environment. I see in this bill no assurance that there will be a deputy minister of forests who will in fact be responsible for forests, who will be able to speak with equal weight with anybody in his department on behalf of forests. I wonder whether this department will now become subject to the selections of attention it may get when the minister appoints a deputy minister of environment. I fear this and I suggest to the government that there should be within the department an equal spokesman for forests as well as for the environment. Those two voices could then be heard in balance, at least, and would not be too far down the line to be listened

to by the minister. They would have direct access to the minister on an equal footing.
There are times of conflict between the environment and the forests, and I suppose New Brunswick is a prime example of that conflict when we talk about budworm spraying. Environmentalists speak with one voice and those who favour protection of the forests speak with another. Unless those two voices are heard on an equal basis by a single minister of a department here in Ottawa, the interests of the environmentalists may prevail rather than the interests of the forests.
As we listened to the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand) yesterday we were concerned by the suggestion in his remarks that we have increased the number of people at Petawawa. This statement on its own suggests to those who may have heard the news or read the speech, without full knowledge of what is going on, that the research station at Petawawa will in fact be doing more research in the same field it has historically done that research than before.
The minister went on to say the government had accepted some of the suggestions of the Conservative party with regard to cutting government spending. He did not go on to say that the Conservative party had suggested, and has done so since I have been associated with this party, that research was a foundation and an investment in a better future. At no time and in no way has any Conservative in this House suggested that we make savings in respect of research unless such research can be proven to be wasteful. Certainly there is no proof that any research done at Petawawa, or any other research establishment, has been wasteful. We, therefore, never recommended cuts in respect of research.
It is for that reason that I wish to draw to the attention of the minister the suggestion that Petawawa will become one of the foremost research establishments in the country. It has long been recognized as the research establishment of Canada, but now it is to be downgraded, regardless of what the minister has said.
There have been many representations made to the minister in this regard. I for one have consistently suggested there should be more research in respect of the budworm situation. I wish to quote from the report of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry proceedings at page 2:15, November 28, 1978. I asked this question of the witnesses of the day and the minister:
-I would like to ask the minister if the department has undertaken an assessment of what would have happened to the forests of New Brunswick if there had been no budworm sprayings since 1952?
The minister's reply was as follows:
I read some reports, Mr. Chairman, and as I recall the conclusion was that if the province of New Brunswick did not spray, they probably would have lost all their forest.
I would qualify that by saying that we were talking at that time of the coniferous forests and not the deciduous forests of New Brunswick. I quoted that to show my support for research in depth in respect of forests. This problem has existed for approximately 30 years. It was first attended to by spraying in 1952, some 27 years ago as of this year. Research has not been

adequate enough to find any way or means of controlling that problem other than by spraying. I do not quarrel with the research effort that has taken place with respect to this subject. I do quarrel with the idea that any forest research be reduced in view of the need for that particular item.
I would like to draw to hon. members' attention the statement made by the hon. member for South Shore which is in the same report of the fisheries and forestry committee dated November 28, 1978. At page 2:24 the hon. member said:
The forest industry in Canada already generates one million jobs, $6 billion in foreign trade and $2 billion in federal and provincial taxes annually. Trade figures indicate that Canada's more favourable balance of payments situation in recent months is due largely to our forestry sector-
I might add to that that the minister who was present at that time corrected the hon. member on page 2:25 of the same report, and said:
It is higher than that, it is about $7.5 billion.
He was referring to the balance of trade which was generated by the forest industry. When we become penny wise and pound foolish with the reduction of research in an industry which is generating $7.5 billion in favourable trade balance, I think we are taking the wrong direction.
We have had conflicting reports from different sources as to its impact. A news release, which does not seem to have a date on it but is headed up "The Minister of Environment Canada", reads:
The goal of achieving more for less will, in this case, be accomplished by consolidateding the work of the Forest Fire Research Institute and the Forest Management Institute, both now located in Ottawa.
I quote again from page 2 of that release, which reads:
After consolidation, the staff of Petawawa will be increased from 78 to over 100. The station will have a budget of $3.5 million. As many as 60 employees of the Ottawa institutes will move to Petawawa. About 50-70 employees both Ottawa and Petawawa will, however, still have to be laid off to achieve the required budget reductions.
If one talks to researchers in the forest industry and asks them when we are going to get results or when they will know what they have accomplished, those researchers will probably say that it may be up to 100 years before the work which they started today will have a known result, in a positive or negative way, for the forest industry. The work which was done at Petawawa, however, and which has been done there for over 60 years, is to be cut back. This means that many of the projects which were started ten to 50 years ago have not yet been brought to a conclusion. The results are not known. Therefore, any cutback in the staff of that research station will result in the frustration of up to 60 years of work on certain projects.
That is not the worst of it. We in our society today are making use of our forests in a way which has never been done before. We are now demanding of our forest soil that it produce a crop on a regular, annual basis. The soil has never had to do that before. If the budworms were to remove an area of coniferous forest from the land, it was of no particular
January 24, 1979

consequence at one time; but if the budworm was to remove an area of forest today, then there would be no jobs tomorrow.
We then come to the problem of how to control our forest industry and its regeneration, what research do we have to direct us as to what trees should be planted and where, according to our reforestation program, which is so necessary to the continuing crop structure required for employment in Canada north and east of the St. Lawrence. Most of that forest is being cropped to the limit of its productive capacity. We must have that research. Therefore, any cutback in that area is detrimental to the long-term, best interests of the industry. It is necessary to know what will grow best on what soil, for example, in New Brunswick, in eastern Quebec and in Nova Scotia.
The government of Nova Scotia undertook a study in a certain area of that province whereby they analysed the soil required for the trees. That study recommended what trees should be grown in what particular region of the province, outlined the number of cords or cubic feet of wood that could be grown per acre in each region, and which regions were not worthy of reforestation or even of consideration in a remunerative way to the forest industry.
This is the kind of work which was being done in Petawawa. This cutback, however, is taking place in spite of the fact that a news release has come out from the Department of the Environment headed, "Lost in the Woods, a Circular Dilemma". It asks why it is that Canada's share of world export markets for forest products has decreased form 31 per cent to 19 per cent in the last 20 years, while the U.S. share has increased from less than 9 per cent to more than 12 per cent. It seems we are going in the opposite direction with a smaller population and with more wood. The news release also asks why the general productivity in the wood products industry in Canada is 15 per cent less than in the U.S., and why it is that Canada with a forest industry that provides direct and indirect employment for nearly one million people, and that contributes almost one-fifth of the nation's exports, finds itself with serious problems emerging with regard to economic supplies of timber. Another pertinent question it asks is why it is that competing products are making inroads into traditional wood markets despite the relatively low energy requirement to process trees into products and despite the potential for industrial self-sufficiency in energy through residue utilization.
The news release goes on to ask why it is that Denmark, a country nearly devoid of timber, uses more wood in public and industrial buildings than we do in Canada. Why is it that building code developments for wood systems lag behind those for alternative materials? It further asks why it is that federally funded research and development at forest product laboratories is about $14 million in the United States and only $7 million in Canada.
All these questions are being asked in light of the fact that we are now cutting back on research in forestry and putting forestry into a secondary position in a department coupled
Government Organization
with environment. These questions are coming from Environment Canada, Mr. Speaker. I could go on to cite a multitude of such questions but I should like to skip ahead to the end of this news release which states:
All of this in spite of the fact that... Hon. Judd Buchanan, Minister of State for Science and Technology announced in parliament in June an ambitious program leading to a national goal to increase R&D in Canada from its present 0.92 per cent (less than half that of Germany, Netherlands, France or U.S.) of gross domestic product to 1.5 per cent by 1983.
Hon. Len Marchand, Minister of State for the Environment, and minister responsible for the Canadian Forestry Service, pledged in a Vancouver speech before the Canadian Institute of Forestry last December:
"I want to assure you now that I have no intention of downplaying the role of the Canadian Forestry Service. If economic restraints make further cuts in my department necessary, I intend to make sure that the Canadian Forestry Service does not suffer. I want to see its role enhanced, in recognition of the high priority I place on the Canadian forest resources."
I should now like to read a portion of a letter written to me by the Public Service Alliance of Canada relating to Petawawa. The relevant portion is as follows:
However, the government still insists on the same $1.5 million cut and the same 70 to 80 people lay-off. With our friends in the Canadian Forestry Service, we now continue our fight to save the government forest research. We hope all our political friends will take up this fight in the House of Commons.
Perhaps that is one of the presentations which were made to the minister and to which he referred.
One of the reasons why an element of the Petawawa operation was saved may have been a telex sent to the Prime Minister by Dean V. J. Nordin, president of the Association of University Forestry Schools of Canada, on September 18, 1978, which reads as follows:
On behalf of all schools of forestry in Canada at the universities of B.C., Alberta, Lakehead, Toronto, Laval, and New Brunswick, I view with deep concern the catastrophic implications for Canadian forestry that will result from reductions announced recently by the federal government. The heads of forestry schools met with the honourable Len Marchand last June 21 and the minister said that he would resist any further damaging reductions to an already depleted and demoralized Canadian forestry service. Unless these new reductions are reviewed and changed there will be enormous and irreparable injury to Canadian forestry. Supporting details follow by letter.
The letter at great length lays clearly on the line to the Prime Minister what the consequences of the reduction will be. Each of the three departments of research which are now located in Petawawa has been effectively emasculated; each of the three research departments has had reductions in personnel and is no longer as effective or as productive as it would otherwise have been. Valuable research personnel have been irretrievably lost.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take a few minutes to participate in this bill on government organization. I should like to comment on some statements made yesterday, first of all by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) who spoke rather in motherhood terms of his support for the gillnetters

January 24, 1979
Government Organization
and trailers of British Columbia. He pointed to a problem brought up recently when the regional office of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment announced that the 150 fathom fishing by the gillnetters in the herring season would be reduced to 50 fathom one net, rather than two nets. The hon. member did not say whether he was in favour of one net or two nets but merely said this was proof that the government was attacking small businessmen. This is nonsense, Mr. Speaker. The only reason I bring it up is to show the difference between responsible representation and nonresponsible representation. Motherhood phrases do very little to assist fishermen faced with a problem.
I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo), who is from Skeena, the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Pearsall) and I met with the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) when this matter was brought to our attention. We pointed out that changes in regulations regarding the herring catch several weeks before the season was to start was very unfair regardless of whether the 50 fathom net is more desirable from a conservation point of view. Before the season begins the gillnetters have purchased their equipment and nets on the basis of existing regulations.
We also pointed out that by reducing the number of nets from two to one, approximately 1,000 people in the fishing industry in British Columbia would be laid off and that, of course, is not desirable. We asked the minister to have discussions on this subject with the fishermen concerned before the regulations were brought in.
I am pleased to report, Mr. Speaker, that today the minister informed us that the director general of the regional office in Vancouver will call a press conference at two o'clock this afternoon regarding the gillnetters. I am sure the recommendations made by the members from British Columbia on this side of the House to the effect that there should be a one-year period for discussion will be taken into account. Certainly not enough time is being allowed to make decisions just before the herring season begins. I understand the minister has accepted the recommendation and I trust a solution to the problem will be found.
Approximately one year ago there was a debate in this House on the question of forming a separate ministry of fisheries. Shortly after that the minister was able to announce that a ministry of fisheries and the oceans would be established. That has a nice ring to it, Mr. Speaker. This finally takes into account the fact that we in Canada have expanded our coastline and that the amount of territory we govern is literally hundreds of thousands of miles with the introduction of the 200-mile limit which was brought in by a Liberal government and the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment.
It gives me some concern, Mr. Speaker, after having established the 200-mile economic zone, which we all agree will benefit the people of Canada, especially in the maritimes and along the west coast-

-to hear that the official opposition is now apparently attempting to balkanize the fishing industry in Canada by turning over jurisdiction which they have supported and increasing the role of the Ministry of Fisheries. They now say that if elected they would take power away from the Ministry of Fisheries and distribute it among the provinces concerned. Instead of talking platitudes about what we have done right or wrong, I would like someone from the opposition to state in this House whether they wish to balkanize the fishing industry in Canada and establish the same sort of regime as that established in the United States of America which has experienced disastrous results. Those of you who have followed the course of fishery policy in the United States I am sure are aware that states have jurisdiction out to 12 miles, the federal government has jurisdiction from the 12-mile limit to 200 miles. But there is a third area of legislation, that of regional councils.
We talk about a fishing war with the United States. There is no doubt in my mind that we got into the situation because the United States, through its three arms of jurisdiction, could not make up its mind as to what it wanted. Signing an agreement with the United States at the present time is very chancy business due to the fact that we are dealing basically with three separate levels of government.
Having said that, I am amazed to learn that apparently a plank of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, if they are put into power, is to turn over the duties of the Minister of Fisheries to the premiers of the provinces in the Atlantic Region so they could have their own fish war. As I said, they would balkanize the fishing industry and I am sure we would have exactly the same results as those that have occurred in the United States, namely a lack of central power to make decisions on behalf of fishermen in general rather than having the proposal which has come forward, and that we would have our own wars among the provinces. I hope that someone from the official opposition will bring up that subject today because I think it is very important. There is no point establishing a fisheries portfolio giving the minister broad powers if at the same time the Conservative party wishes to disband it as soon as they are elected.
There is no question in mind, Mr. Speaker, that since 1974 a revolution has occurred regarding the fisheries industry of Canada. Many of us will recall that prior to the 1974 election a meeting was held in Caracas, Venezuela, which was really the forerunner of the Law of the Sea process that has allowed us to go forward to 1978, when many of the coastal states have achieved sovereignty over the waters adjacent to them through the 200-mile economic zone.
Fishermen from British Columbia have asked me why we had not gone into massive hatchery programs prior to the proclamation of the 200-mile economic zone. They have asked why the government has been slow to meet the needs of fishermen in British Columbia. Let us make it very clear in the House that it would have been very foolish, before we had
January 24, 1979

obtained sovereignty over our coastal waters, to have spent hundreds of millions of dollars for the benefit of distant water fishing fleets to harvest a resource that is costing Canada literally millions of dollars. It would have been utter foolishness to have money spent by the people of Canada for the benefit of distant water fishing fleets.
I believe very strongly that the policy that has been carried out by this minister has been correct, first of all establishing sovereignty over coastal waters and ensuring that money spent by the people of Canada for the enhancement of fish stocks will benefit the people of Canada rather than other nations with distant water fishing fleets. In that regard I totally agree with the minister.
Yesterday the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) made reference to a statement apparently originating from the Fisheries Council of Canada to the effect that the minister should resign his portfolio. However, the hon. member for South Shore did not mention that while some leaders of the fishing industry demanded the removal of the minister last fall, Richard Cashin, president of the Newfoundland Fishermen's Union, sent a protest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). If I may quote from that protest, it reads:
Romeo LeBlanc has established himself in the eyes of fishermen of Newfoundland and I believe all over eastern Canada as no other fishery minister has probably since confederation.
There are many important policy areas where LeBlanc is moving in the right direction and this is a critical period for fishermen. Sincerely hope you will see fit to keep him in fishery.
I would like to pose a question. When was the last time, Mr. Speaker, that you heard of a labour leader springing to the defence of a Liberal cabinet leader? It does not happen very often. As I said, a revolution has occurred in Canada since the 1974 meeting of the Law of the Sea in Caracas, Venezuela.
I believe we have done a very poor job of giving credit for that revolution to the members of the Canadian delegation who so ably represented us in Geneva, New York and Caracas. 1 am referring to people such as Allan Beesley, head of the Canadian delegation, Len Legault, Dr. Crosby and Dr. Needier, who recently retired. I say this because we as politicians like to take credit for things that are done on behalf of the Government of Canada, but sometimes we do not realize the importance of people like Allan Beesley and Dr. Needier. Anyone who has paid close attention to the Law of the Sea Conference realizes that Canada has played a role in that conference disproportionate to our population and to the power we have as an international force. It goes without saying that Canada has been the glue that has held the Law of the Sea Conference together and many of the proposals that are coming forward regarding the oceans and deep seabed mining are proposals which have been brought forward by the Government of Canada through its very able representatives.
I would like to use these few minutes to state publicly that the Canadian people owe a great deal to these negotiators. In addition to that I would like to say that the Law of the Sea Conference owes a great deal to Canada. It is my sincere opinion that this particular conference would have disbanded years ago if there had not been someone who could have talked
Government Organization
to all parties involved and attempted to find a common ground to continue negotiations.
We talk about the structure of setting up a department of fisheries and the oceans. In a similar debate a year ago I said that we should have a separate department recognizing the fact that the Department of Fisheries, along with its minister, is an area with great potential growth. I am sure that the Minister of Fisheries is on occasion frustrated because he knows that there is probably greater potential growth in his department than in any other area. He has one of the lowest budgets. I am sure that if some of us had our way we would have greater input of money into the Department of Fisheries, perhaps coming from some of the non-productive departments to what is a growth department.
1 do not believe there is any doubt either in the minister's mind or in my mind that, as we use land masses to their full potential in providing food for an ever increasing world population, at some point in the future the world will have to turn to the oceans as a source of nourishment. If one is mercenary, one would have to say that those engaged in the fishing industry and related aquaculture industries in Canada have the greatest potential for growth, if only because distant foreign fishing fleets can no longer supply their people with fish they normally catch off the coasts of Canada, the United States and South America.
We in western Canada are seeing the results of the 200-mile economic zone. Take, for example, the herring industry, one in which few people wanted to participate until a few years ago because they could not earn enough money to make it worth while. Most of the catch was ground up for fertilizer or made into cat and dog food. It was used for every purpose except feeding people. There was no other market for it. Today, because of the 200-mile zone, the situation has changed. This year the herring roe fishery in British Columbia will be a $100 million industry. This sum will go into the pockets of fishermen, processors and others in the Pacific region, though a few years ago the commercial returns from this product were so negligible that no one talked about them. Where is the herring going? It is going to the Japanese who are no longer able to harvest this species in Canadian waters or other waters they have traditionally fished.
I certainly bear no malice toward Japan or any other country, but for the first time in the history of the fishing industry we have been able to establish sovereignty over waters which are adjacent to Canada, and as a result we are now seeing a breakthrough of tremendous importance. We shall be able not only to harvest but to manage these resources on a sustained yield basis. This will prove to be better for the countries purchasing fish from us because hitherto there had been a rape of the ocean's resources. It was like a piece of agricultural land that nobody owned and everyone could try to profit from. We now have under our control resource management programs which will benefit not only the people of Canada, fishermen in particular, but countries all over the

January 24, 1979
Government Organization
world which cannot grow sufficient food on their own land and which have to rely on the fisheries for sustenance. They will now have a constant supply available to them.
The breakthrough I am talking about extends not only to herring roe and salmon. For the first time we are seeing the development of new possibilities. In British Columbia, dogfish are the bane of commercial fishermen because they tear up the nets and are, in general, of no use to our fleet. Today, though, a market has been found for them in Europe and catching them is a profitable undertaking. This new market will provide our fishermen with additional income while ridding the sea of a species which is damaging to salmon stocks as well as to the nets of commercial operators.

I do not know whether the government considers a session as a political race to be won and feels that it has to hide its cards, keeping some surprises till the end, or whether it is so devoid of imagination at the beginning of a session that it is unable to introduce any specific basic issue which would enable the House to launch serious and productive debates, but it is

always the same thing. The first bill with which we are dealing today is an indisputable proof of that never-ceasing repetition of the procedure used in previous years.
Whoever reads Bill C-35, respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, gets the impression that the officials responsible for drafting this bill have not yet recovered from the lethargy of the festive season. In fact, for the past few years and especially last summer, when there were strong rumours of election, the present government intended to establish a department of fisheries separate from the department of environment. Finally, today, although it is a bit late since it is about to go to the people, the government introduces this bill as the first and main subject for debate. Some would say that we are nearing election time. Such a legislation is certainly a sign that we shall have an election within the next few months, as surely as a cloudy sky announces a rainfall.
Which serves to confirm what we the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada have always claimed, namely that the old parties always administer the country with an eye on the electorate, to gain votes so to speak, without giving much consideration to the nation's welfare. To make a long story short, why did the government not keep the name of the fisheries department and simply add the name of oceans, since this is particularly the same bill amended by the same minister, perhaps with a new dressing? For the public servants, of course, it is a question of doing something new, of hiring more people and of getting a larger budget.
Mr. Speaker, even though the present government would have us believe that the numerous subjects dealt with in Bill C-35 amount only to a bunch of administrative details, because that is its intention in introducing that package deal, I would like to try to clarify some very important points which are covered in that bill concerning areas such as fisheries, environment, research and development, and changes in electoral constituencies. So, for the benefit of the public, I will try to make clear what the civil servants have taken so much time to make obscure.
First of all, I would like to remind hon. members that the establishment of the department of fisheries and oceans as a separate entity from the Department of Environment is an electoral promise which goes back more than four years. If we consider the whole question of the development of our underwater natural resources as well as the question of the extension of our territorial limit to 200 miles from our coasts, I think that the new department of fisheries and oceans will have a very important role to play in the future, so much so that its establishment, its duties and responsibilities should have come under a separate bill instead of being just a part of a pre-election omnibus package which is introduced and passed with great pressure to the prejudice of all Canadians. From the

point of view of the procedure, Mr. Speaker, this bill is abominable if we consider that part I deals with the establishment of the new department of fisheries and oceans and that it is only at the very end of the bill, more precisely in part IX, after having heard about the public service, the electoral legislation, research councils and parliamentary secretaries, that at last we can learn how that new department is going to be financed. There are two important changes in part II of the bill. First the fisheries and oceans research advisory council is substituted for the fisheries research board.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that in addition to changing the name of this agency to make it fit with the department's new name, the government took pains to include the word "advisory" which was not there before. The second significant change is the increase in the number of members of the council from 18 to 24. The members are recruited in the public service, in universities and teaching establishments, in industries and among the general public. All this is very nice, but what good will it do to pay civil servants to draft bills and to hire more members for a council which the government pointedly calls "advisory", meaning that its only function will be to advise the minister?
For almost two years now agencies like the Canadian Association of University Teachers and the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies have been constantly trying to explain to this government that such advisory bodies should become executive agencies with their own powers and that they should not depend only on inefficient ministers or general administrators of the same type. The public also requested larger representation of the Canadian scientific community on those advisory bodies, and what is the government bringing us today? It announces an increase in the membership of the new advisory body.
But what will be the proportion of members coming from universities, industry and the public service? We still do not know. I refer hon. members on the government side to the debates of March 7, April 17 and December 1, 1978, when hon. members of our party made a clear description of the lamentable condition of research and development in Canada. What solution is proposed? More members coming from we do not know where to sit on a board which has no executive power.
In the third part, it is a good thing the government has at long last recognized that the question of the environment calls for a separate department and established such a department as an autonomous body in Part III of Bill C-35. However, we of the Social Credit Party of Canada believe the powers and functions attributed to the Department of the Environment in the bill before the House are very limited and in fact too limited. In fact, in subclause 6(c) the minister is depicted as an adviser to the heads of various departments and other agen-

cies. Would it not have been better to establish a code for the evaluation of negative goods based on abundant data relating to the pollution of the environment which we have in hand and to give the Minister of the Environment the responsibility to apply this code? It is high time our country adopts such a code and applies it to all commercial and industrial development rather than hoping thaf toothless tigers will protect our environment. Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise in support of Bill C-35, particularly that part of the bill dealing with the reorganization of the legislative arm of the government by creating a separate department of fisheries and oceans. I think the legislative paper is both clear and straightforward. Based on comments made by members of all parties in this House over a year, it is a progressive measure that seems satisfactory to everyone. Bill C-35 proposes to create a department to be called the department of fisheries and oceans. The duties, powers and functions of the department will include all matters over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, not by law assigned to any other department, or agency of the Government of Canada, relating to (1) sea coast and inland fisheries, (2) fishing and recreational harbours, (3) hydrography and marine sciences.

-and:
(b) such other matters over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction relating to oceans as are by law assigned to the minister.
Part II of the bill provides for amendment or repeal of certain sections of the Fisheries Research Board Act to allow the replacement of the old Fisheries Research Board with a new fisheries and oceans research advisory council. This council will advise and report directly to the minister. The majority of its members would normally be scientists, but to answer right away hon. members of the New Democratic Party

mainly, that fishermen should be represented, I can assure them they will be. In fact, the word "industry" in my understanding would include both fishermen and, of course, processors.
The council will then advise the minister in matters relating to fisheries research and the marine sciences, including technological developments in those fields, the scope and adequacy of science policies and programs of the department of fisheries and oceans, having regard to the duties and functions of that department, the science policy and international obligations of the Government of Canada, and the co-ordination of research and development programs in the field of fisheries research and the marine sciences.
In a nutshell, the establishment by this bill of the new department and council will provide a clearcut administrative and policy framework for carrying out the federal government's constitutional mandate for "seacoast and inland fisheries", including our fisheries management and ocean science responsibilities, and administration of the legislation listed in schedule I of the bill.
There are other related, consequential amendments which are included in schedule II to ensure that the mandate of the minister of fisheries and oceans is appropriately recognized in other legislation.
I feel it would be worth while at this time to cast a backward glance at events of the past decade to examine why this government took the step it did in creating a federal department of the environment in 1971, and decided to include in it the then department of fisheries and forestry. The overriding reason at that time for the creation of an environment department was the absence of a national focal point for environmental concerns and the lack of a strong federal organization to co-ordinate and lead the fight against encroaching pollution of the environment.
One of the events that occurred at that time was the discovery of mercury contamination in the Great Lakes and elsewhere which provided a dramatic example of the need for swift and effective action by the senior government. It should be borne in mind that at that time no provincial government has an environmental department to cope adequately with the situations which were, to many people's surprise, arising. Even worse, there was very little environmental legislation on the books that could be used to stop or roll back pollution except for the Fisheries Act. The Fathers of Confederation in their wisdom had included anti-pollution provisions in the Fisheries Act when it was passed into law more than a century ago, and those provisions, beefed up by stiffening the penalties for polluting any water where there was fish life, were used very effectively in the war against pollution in the early 1970s.
Among our renewable natural resources the fisheries, of course, stood to lose the most from the effects of pollution of our lakes, rivers and oceans. The Fisheries Act served as an invaluable stop-gap until other environmental protection legislation could be put into place, and until provincial governments were able to organize their own environmental departments and join the attack at the provincial level.

The key to rational management of the offshore fisheries resource was, of course, extended jurisdiction. Canada unilaterally introduced a 200-mile fishing zone on its east and west coasts on January 1, 1977. Here 1 should like to pay homage to my own colleages in cabinet, particularly the former secretary of state for external affairs, the present government House leader, and his successor, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) and distinguished representative of Newfoundland. This declaration of the 200-mile zone was without doubt a milestone in Canada's fishing history, and I believe marked the turning point in the furtunes of the industry.
Now, with effective management control over most of the offshore fishing grounds, backed by successfully negotiated bilateral agreements with countries that traditionally fished off our coasts, a new era of prosperity looms on the horizon for Canada's hard-pressed fishing communities. Significantly, in the year 1977 the total market value of Canada's fisheries topped the $1 billion mark. Fisheries is getting to be big business, and it is also abundantly clear that the fisheries department with its many added responsibilities should re-emerge as a separate entity.
OO)
Thus it was that in the fall of 1977 the Prime Minister announced the government's intention to set up a new department to look after Canada's fisheries. Wheels were set in motion to accomplish this and the necessary legislation was placed before the House last June. Unfortunately, time ran out on us and the bill died on the order paper. In any case, if anyone should be wondering, I might add at this point that we have not been sitting around twiddling our thumbs waiting for the passage of the bill. Anticipating the split in the department, my officials have been busily occupied with sorting out the administrative arrangements and the transfer of responsibilities which such an action would involve.
Government Organization
Much of the machinery necessary for fisheries to function as a separate department is now in place. With the approval of this House and the Senate, the new department will be known as the department of fisheries and oceans. An associate deputy minister has already been appointed-he is now well settled in his job-and a senior management structure in the new department has been developed. Of course, the associate deputy minister would become the new deputy minister with the passage of the legislation.
There are now four assistant deputy ministers: one responsible for the central, inland and western fisheries, one for the eastern fishery, one for the ocean and aquatic sciences, and a new assistant deputy minister concentrating on marketing and developmental aspects. I might add that the officials of both sectors, the Department of the Environment and the Department of Fisheries, worked well together, and I am sure are ready to continue doing so because there will always be a close relationship between those who are involved in the protection of the environment and those who are working in fisheries.
The name "fisheries and oceans" was chosen deliberately to indicate that the new department's make-up includes a marine science component. This is not something that has been tacked on as an afterthought. The fisheries are part of the ocean's eco-system, and in order to manage them effectively the input of many disciplines of marine science is absolutely essential.
Perhaps I could best define this department by pointing out the objectives of the ocean and aquatic sciences sector. Firstly, it is to conduct on a national basis research into physical, chemical and biological oceanography to gain a better understanding of the marine and fresh water environments.
Secondly, it is to support through this program the management of marine and fresh water resources, the enhancement and protection of marine and fresh water environmental quality, and the safe, orderly and efficient conduct of shipping in Canadian waters and those areas of the ocean of direct interest to Canada.
A third objective of OAS is to contribute to national capability in fisheries and marine science through the development and transfer of ocean technology. It has also been given the provision of direct financial aid to qualified university research projects through the subvention program, and the implementation of a national fisheries and marine scientific information and publications policy.
Last but by no means the least of the OAS functions is to ensure that adequate hydrographic data, charts and publications are available as and when needed to meet the needs of navigation in all Canadian waters. This is of direct benefit to commercial fishermen as well as to marine fishing in general, and to the ever increasing population of pleasure boaters in this country.
It is perhaps worth mentioning that the ocean and aquatic sciences sector had its origin back in 1959 as part of the past fisheries research board of Canada, when it was known as the division of oceanographic research. At that time it used the administrative and ship support arm of the Canadian hydro-

graphic service. Subsequently the group was attached to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and more recently became part of the fisheries and marine service within the environment department. Thus it may be claimed that OAS has turned full circle and is back where it started from.
The shaping of a new department has provided the government with an opportunity to take a good, hard look at fisheries needs as they currently exist throughout Canada and at what may be needed for the future. Efficient and economically sound management of the fisheries-whether salt water or fresh water-is obviously the basic concern of any fisheries department.
Fisheries management, however, entails a lot more than merely setting catch quotas and licensing fishermen. It requires science and research, a knowledge of what, where and when to fish, an understanding of the very complex factors which affect stock, health and abundance. It involves not only controlling how much fish is harvested, but also attempting to spread that fish throughout the year to keep processing plants fully occupied. It means devising methods to increase the natural or artificial production of fish, such as the multi-million dollar salmonid enhancement program now in top gear in British Columbia. It involves measures to protect and, where necessary, rehabilitate fisheries habitats-the streams, estuaries and other places where fish spawn and spend their early life. It means coming up with programs to protect the fisheries resource, and that includes combating the poaching of valuable species such as salmon and lobster.
Incidentally, with the help of this parliament, two amendments were put into the Fisheries Act which have been very helpful in the area of habitat protection and stricter or stronger measures against illegal fishing. The fishermen themselves are now discovering that the resource is also theirs to protect. In Prince Edward Island a very positive experiment was tried by the fishermen during the last season and on their own estimate the amount of poaching dropped substantially in the lobster fishery. Other fishermen groups, with this example in mind, are suggesting that they too should have a role in the protection of their own resource. I know that this problem is less serious in certain provinces, especially Newfoundland where the sacredness of the fishery is recognized very broadly.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the House, I might spend a few minutes speaking about the current fate of Canada's fisheries. Occasionally there are cries of outraged protest from the media or from politicians that Canada is not taking full advantage of our opportunities under the 200-mile limit. Sometimes these protests are accompanied by calls to cash in on this wonderful new bonanza by vastly expanding the fishing fleet. In both cases these protests are from people who have not taken the trouble to study the situation, or have chosen to ignore the facts for whatever reason.
Let us look at some of the facts. On the fishing grounds of British Columbia full-time fishermen earn stable, responsible and respectable incomes. Pacific salmon already are the most valuable fish in Canada. Our federal salmonid enchancement program with British Columbia's excellent co-operation will

double the number of salmon by the 1990s. In Pacific ground-fish we can eventually increase our catches four times. I have not mentioned it but the hon. member for Commox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) has mentioned the very lucrative herring roe fishery.
On the prairies the federal Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation continues to provide marketing stability. In the interior and on the coasts federal-provincial co-operation in the recreational fishing industry has increased markedly. On the Atlantic coast, despite strong conservation measures, fishermen's incomes have increased 50 per cent in recent years. From 1974 through to 1977 landings rose some 20 per cent and landed value rose over 50 per cent. Provisional figures for 1978 show landings are up another 13 per cent and value is up a healthy 37 per cent over 1977.
Besides the new dollars there is a new feeling of stability about the fishery. Those of us who read the economic review of the different provinces in the Globe and Mail business supplement were, I am sure, impressed of find that in most provinces fisheries was singled out as an area of development and an area of quite dramatic progress. Catches are more reliable and plant work is steadier and is stretching over more of the year. There is growth in fishermen's organizations. Fishermen have gained status in the community. No longer is the fishery the employer of last resort. The potential for job increases on the Atlantic coast is higher in processing than in fishing-20,000 or more new jobs is not unlikely.
By 1985 we could double our catch of Atlantic groundfish. But this is not only a function of more boats. Partly, bigger landings will come from bigger catch rates per boat. The estimated doubling of our groundfish catch depends also on our making use of species such as grenadier and hake that we now ignore.
Except in northern cod, it is hard to foresee fleet expansion for our traditional fisheries, either from growth in fish stocks or from displacement of foreign effort. As fish stocks increase, a fleet the size of our existing one can take much larger catches-and, in fact, our fleet was doing so ten years ago.
In 1977 we took 76 per cent of traditional groundfish and herring on the Atlantic coast, including waters both inside and outside the 200-mile limit. Of all finfish last year, including both the species our fishermen seek and those they ignore, and including fish both inside and outside the limit, and taking into account the rights of France in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, we caught about 60 per cent. The percentage is even higher off Nova Scotia.
Atlantic fish prices have never been so high. Atlantic landed value has risen from $224 million in 1976 to $280 million in 1977. The idea of massive fleet expansion for traditional species-and I want to be very clear on this-is a pipe dream. In the northern cod fishery and in underutilized species there could be expansion. But using underutilized species to expand our fleet and catch to their full potential depends on being able to sell what we catch. Until there is some dramatic break-

through in product or market development-and these are largely areas of responsibility of industry and the provinces-it is difficult to look quickly at the day when the foreign fishing fleet will have left Canadian shores.
To those who advocate a policy of removing all foreign fishing from the Canadian zone, I point out that this is a very short-term and short-sighted policy because it does not take into account two very important protections which we require, and these are the interest of Canada outside the 200-mile zone on the east coast-and Newfoundland is aware of this problem-and, of course, the fate of the Atlantic and Pacific salmon on the high seas. We need some negotiating power to protect our vital interest in this species.
I might also say that access to the Canadian zone can be discussed and negotiated with the full knowledge of all the segments of the industry. That access can be granted in exchange for other benefits such as markets which, of course, Canada should diversify because of our overdependency on the United States market.
Some hon. members have made comments to which I should like to refer briefly, with your permission, Mr. Speaker. On the matter of fleet expansion and freezer trawlers the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) forgot to underline that our existing fleet on the east coast could take at least 50 per cent more fish than it is taking. A factory freezer trawler could probably triple what our best trawlers now catch and some 90 times what the inshore longliner can catch. The implications respecting the over-all structure of the industry, and in particular the potential hazard posed to the livelihood of inshore and offshore fishermen, are obvious to me.
In the matter of freezer trawlers, of the six applications received in 1979, all are contingent upon access to traditional species which our present fleet is not only able to catch but where the catch rate could mean more fish for our fishermen. Those applications are contingent upon access to those traditional species and in many cases they require financial investment and involvement by foreign countries.
The hon. member has taken as his text a letter from the Fisheries Council of Canada. I think he and I separate clearly on this issue. I have made it clear that in the disposal of this common property resource, which is held in trust by the Government of Canada on behalf of the people of Canada, the first interest that has to be considered-and as long as I am the minister the first interest that is considered-is the interest of fishermen, starting with those who live in the communities that are the most isolated and whose mobility is the most limited. It was in the name of the small coastal communities and the small fishermen who could not compete with the foreign fishing fleets that we argued successfully with the rest of the world that Canada should manage the 200-mile zone.
If the hon. member wants to take the letter of the Fisheries Council as his text, I will take as my text a letter from the Fishermen's Union of Newfoundland dated April 5, 1978, which stated that their "basic principles are ... a go slow approach in the acquisition of factory ships." On this position our difference of views is quite clear.

The hon. member also talked about a long-term policy. I have tabled a document published in 1976 which, barring some adjustment required because of scientific readjustment, is, I think, perfectly valid today. This document established objectives and strategies for the development of Canada's fisheries. In resource management it covered important issues such as the extension of jurisdiction and effective management of the resource to ensure not only a sustainable yield but also the best social and economic use.
Regarding harvesting, the document advocates the need for systems of balanced access to ensure stability of the resource and improved incomes for fishermen. It also advocates improving fishing gear and practices and ensuring the viability of appropriate fleets depending on the nature of the fishery.
In processing, the document advocates quality, full utilization of the resource and arranging for the distribution of catches, particularly during glut periods, to plants in areas where catches are low in order to extend the working time of the plant.
In marketing, the document asked that we ensure competence to take advantage of dramatically changing international market patterns and that we improve our international competitive position through an improved co-ordination and consolidation of exporters.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that the Fisheries Council has created a voluntary organization in the area of market co-ordination, but we are a far distance from our best competitors- and these are not socialist states but free enterprise types of government-who have consolidated their marketing efforts and do not see companies competing among themselves to the advantage of the buyers in markets as strategic as that of the United States.
The hon. member and I also separate on a number of other issues, Mr. Speaker. In the area of technological labs he made an impassioned plea for me to reconsider, but he also established his plea on some rather weak information. The actual number involved in the cutbacks is 30, of which 20 are in the scientific and technical categories, 14 in Halifax, six in Vancouver, the remainder being support staff. The programs affected are those related to packaging, storage of fisheries products, work on utilization of marine oils, and some study on paralytic shellfish poisoning and reproductive biochemistry. We have, however, retained a nucleus of expertise in all these areas. The reduced programs largely benefit the processing industry.
I am looking for the figures which would indicate that during 1978, for instance, the National Sea Company shares increased fivefold in value, from $4.33 to $21. The industry can now afford to do some of its own research and development work in this area, especially with some of the tax benefits that they can receive from the policies of this government. For proof of this, if we check the financial pages, as I have indicated, we will see that those companies which are accounting publicly are showing a fairly healthy picture. The depart-

I should like to tell the minister what the minister of fisheries for Newfoundland, the hon. Walter Carter, had to say on the question of jurisdiction in a speech he made on November 13, 1978. I put it on the record not because it represents the position of the minister of fisheries in Newfoundland, but because it accurately represents the position taken by this party. He said:
We believe that in terms of our respective fiscal responsibility for the provision of fishery and marine related facilities the provincial and federal roles are clearly defined under the BNA Act and while we do not intend to look for anything more than is ours by right we will expect to receive nothing else. We trust federal authorities will fulfil their responsibilities to the letter, and by so doing they will be joining us in the great revolution for the Newfoundland fishery.
That is a clear statement of the position of the province of Newfoundland and it happens to represent in the plainest terms the unambiguous position taken by this party. We are not suggesting, to use the term employed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that we should balkanize the fisheries and take away the jurisdiction of the federal government. What we are saying is that the federal government has a role to play as defined in the constitution, that the provinces have a role to play as defined in the constitution, and that the Fathers of Confederation, in their wisdom, intended that both authorities work together-that they should consult and co-operate, that they should not confront each other or compete with each other as seems to be the case today.
