In these circumstances I have to confess I was somewhat disappointed at the speech given by the Minister of Fisheries. I had hoped to hear the minister give us an outline of his aspirations, of his plans for the future designed to ensure the orderly growth of the industry, realizing, of course, that the achievement of maximum growth along lines which would produce most benefit for our fishermen would require co-operation among all those concerned. I had hoped the minister would have told us how he intended to pursue these commendable and necessary objectives. He failed to do so. I trust that on another occasion he will make up for this serious shortcoming.
Perhaps the reason he did not do so had to do with the nature of the debate in which we are engaged. After all, we are not dealing with a fisheries bill. We are not dealing with a bill calling for the establishment of a new department of fisheries. We are dealing with an omnibus bill. I would be in order if I were to make a speech on a whole range of subjects. The bill deals not only with oceans and fisheries and with the new advisory board; it also deals with the Department of the Environment, Canadian Patents and Development Limited, the representation commissioner, the Medical Research Council, the National Research Council, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, and parliamentary secretaries.
I make reference to the omnibus nature of the bill because we are as anxious as the minister to get the new department of fisheries and oceans on the road. We are anxious to get her launched, christened and out to sea; but then the government puts obstacles like this in our way. Forestry, environmental matters, the representation commissioner, elections, the Medical Research Council, research and development and all these things open up areas of very important debate. I am just concerned that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), who I am sorry to say has never placed the question of fisheries in a very high priority, will perhaps take note of the fact that debate is not going quickly enough, is not going to his satisfaction and not fitting into his timetable, and say to his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment: "I am sorry, Romeo, but I have to withdraw that bill; we have to get on to something else". That would be very regrettable.

The government could have brought in a bill prior to the recess to set up a department of fisheries and oceans, and we would have passed it in a few days. We would have given it second reading in a few days because we would have wanted to use that opportunity to have a full-scale debate in this House on the very important subject of the fishing industry and the future of the fishery in Canada.
The fishing industry is vitally important to many of us, and such a debate would have given the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment an opportunity to make a clearcut policy statement and to open the debate with that kind of statement. We would have a chance to respond constructively, but instead the Deputy Prime Minister introduces a bill to amend the Government Organization Act to reorganize the Government of Canada, we have a response from my learned colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), who in our party has responsibility for matters relating to the organization of the Government of Canada, we get a response from the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand), and all kinds of other responses. The result is that we have a very disjointed debate on the fishing industry, and that is regrettable. The bill might even be withdrawn, and the poor old Department of Fisheries would have to struggle on without having legal sanction for its very existence.
We do not question the right of the minister to proceed. Indeed, we want him to. But I know that the fact that the new department has not been given sanction by law has resulted in a morale problem. People in the Department of Fisheries are not exactly happy that the new department has not been officially established.
I want to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the very capable and dedicated men and women in the fisheries service of Canada, which is what we have at the present time, who will make up the nucleus and form the organization of the new department of fisheries and oceans. They have demonstrated their dedication time and time again, and they have certainly demonstrated their capabilities time and time again. I can speak of no better example than the people who work in the fishery service in my own province of Newfoundland, right from the director, Mr. Cowley, who was a school mate of mine and is one of the outstanding young public servants in Canada and certainly one of the most capable, to his entire staff. The minister nods his agreement that they are a tremendous organization. They are certainly a credit to the Government of Canada and a credit to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment, who recognizes their capabilities and their dedication.
However, it is regrettable that their full potential has not really been harnessed by the government. That is because of something I referred to a few moments ago, the propensity of this government to downgrade the whole fishing industry. We are paying the price, and we have paid the price. I think of what has been done with the fisheries department since 1968 when this government came to power and, indeed, since 1963 when the government of the right honourable, late and great Lester Pearson came to power. The Department of Fisheries

was disestablished and became the department of fisheries and forestry, humourously called the "department of fish and chips".
Then we had the new Department of the Environment established under the direction of a former member of this House from British Columbia. The result of the establishment of the new Department of Fisheries and the Environment was a downgrading of the role of the fishery component at a time when we should have been planning for the day when we would be able to realize jurisdiction over the 200-mile limit. They saw what was coming and prepared for it by increasing the surveillance and rescue capability of the U.S. coastguard. They ordered new ships, new aircraft and new facilities for their coastguard in preparation for the day when they would have jurisdiction over a 200-mile economic zone.

I suspect that if the government is given a new lease on life, which is doubtful, then even perhaps in the final days of the life of this government they might get around to implementing it. It is a good program, one whose time has come.
I can talk about new species development, the development of new markets, our relationship with the common market and the tariff protection of the common market against our fish, which speaks to the dependence of our industry on the east coast on the U.S. market. I can talk about new marketing techniques, taking full advantage of the Asian market. The Japanese are in a position to buy fish from us if we can get it to them frozen or chilled. They are prepared to pay the price for it. We are not actively pursuing that, or at least I am not aware of it if we are.
The People's Republic of China together with Japan will take all of the squid we can produce. The lowly squid holds great promise as a new species for bringing in new returns to our fishermen. I remember the time in Newfoundland when squid was used as a fertilizer; it was a nuisance. Now it is a much sought after food by Oriental people and by some European people. It is a matter of great regret to me to see year after year thousands and thousands of pounds of squid rotting on beaches for lack of holding facilities, for lack of marketing capability and for lack of marketing initiative to get that squid on to the market where there is a great demand for it.

It is excellent, by the way. I would commend squid to my colleague, the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin). Not only is it delicious but it is highly nutritious if properly prepared.
I found myself in agreement, much to the chagrin of my colleagues, with the deal that was made by the Newfoundland fishermen's union to sell squid and mackerel to the east Europeans. It is a market that we had not developed. Not a pound of mackerel had been sold in Newfoundland until that deal was made. So far as squid is concerned, if that deal has the effect of stimulating new marketing initiatives and getting the trade out of its complacency with respect to traditional markets and getting after these markets, then it was an even better deal than I suggested it was. I give the minister full

credit for giving them the licence to do so and 1 give the Newfoundland fish union and the allied workers' union and their president full credit for taking advantage of it.
What are we doing when we talk about selling squid? We are talking about unprocessed fish; there is no processing involved. They are merely selling their products to some foreigner who is buying them directly, and we are just eliminating the broker who usually acts on behalf of the foreign purchaser. However, I would not like to see that as a built-in part of our system because I suspect that ultimately it would destroy the union. After all, the major responsibility of the union is to act as a bargaining agent collectively for the fishermen it represents in dealing with the fish trade, and it could hardly do that if it found itself in that kind of conflict of interest position whereby the very people it had to bargain with collectively on behalf of the fishermen were competing with them for certain markets. So I know it will not become a permanent situation in this country.
The minister spoke about this plan of his which he released today for the first time.

If it is a public document, then perhaps he can explain to us why he found it necessary to table it today. If the document is in the public domain, and I take his word for it, then why did he table it today as part of his speech? I suspect he did so in order to get at his colleagues in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland who had been pressing the minister and the government with respect to a plan for the development of the fisheries in the Atlantic provinces.
He knows, for example, that the government of Newfoundland has an excellent program, which it announced a short time ago, which it brought to the attention of the minister over a year ago and which was formulated in co-operation with the officials of the minister's department. It is a program which entails half a billion dollars in expenditures, a program that cannot possibly succeed without the good will and co-operation of the federal government. I can say to you now, Mr. Speaker, that that good will and co-operation will be forthcoming, because come the next election, when we form the government, we will be only too glad to co-operate with them. I look forward to seeing the present minister over here as the fisheries critic. He will make an excellent fisheries critic. I say to you, sir, that the program will succeed because it will receive the co-operation of the federal government.
It is the constitutional responsibility of the Government of Canada to provide services to the industry, and that speaks again to the low priority of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment in terms of government expenditures. Where do they cut when they have an austerity program? They cut the budget of the small craft harbours division of the fisheries service so that we cannot have our wharves repaired or our breakwaters extended and the facilities looked after. That happens year after year. The result is that the onshore infrastructure of the industry in terms of wharves, breakwaters, slipways and so on is in a sad state of repair. Again its speaks
to the lack of planning and lack of foresight in preparing for the day when the industry will come into its own as a result of the 200-mile limit.
One of the reasons I believe it is so essential, vital and crucial for the industry to have the department re-established on its own once again is its budgetary problems. After all, when the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) speaks in terms of his budget with respect to the Treasury Board, he has to go under the umbrella of the Department of the Environment and compete with the various services that make up that department. The result is that the subservices within the fisheries service, such as small craft harbours, usually are short-changed. The result is, of course, that we as an industry suffer the consequence. I hope that all of these things can come together.
I wanted today, Mr. Speaker, to pay tribute to the Premier of Newfoundland who has announced his retirement, and perhaps I can do so in the few moments I have left. He was a former distinguished member of the House. If there is one thing that can be said and will be said that distinguishes the administration of Frank Moores from any other administration in Newfoundland, it is its emphasis on the fishing industry and its importance to the future of Newfoundland. He turned it around when he became premier and took a positive approach as the government to the industry. The result is that our people now have a confidence in the industry which they have never had before. They approach it in a positive way. The whole population of the province feels positive about the industry and the potential it has to provide jobs for our people and careers for our young people.
I would have liked to have had an opportunity to talk about new species development, our relationship with the common market and what this means in terms of reducing our dependence on the U.S. market. I would like to talk about the saltfish sector and about the criminal situation which prevails with respect to salmon and the fact that the poachers are having a field day. The dynamiters are at work year after year, destroying ton after ton of salmon as they go up the rivers to spawn, because of the lack of funds on the part of the department to provide guardian protection on these rivers. I think that is criminal. If any other country had the potential we had in terms of Atlantic salmon, both as a commercial and sports fishery, it would not hesitate to put the dollars in there to protect this magnificent fish from poachers who are destroying it.
Unfortunately the clock has intervened, but in my final words I should like to say that I hope this bill will be referred, not to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, but to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, where it will receive the examination and attention which the fisheries part of the bill so justly deserves.
